activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Madelyn had on her party dress. It was red with white dots. She wanted to sleep in it. "I wish to wear my dress to bed," she said.

Daddy shook his head. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in," he said. Madelyn pouted. Then she looked at her soft pajamas. They had wild monkeys on them. She touched the dress. It was stiff. She touched the pajamas. They were soft and cozy.

"I will try the monkeys," she said. Daddy helped her pull off the dress. She wiggled into the pajamas. She ate her apple slice first. Then she brushed her teeth. She climbed into bed. The soft monkeys hugged her arms. Her eyes closed fast.

"Goodnight, monkeys," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Henri ran up the steps to Grandma's house. Today was a big day. His new baby sister was here! He wanted to hold her more than anything. But Mom said he had to sit very still on the couch. That felt hard.

Henri sat. He made his body as still as a frozen pond. Grandma put the baby on his lap. The baby was so small. Her hand opened and closed. Henri did not know what to do. Then Mom said, "Try putting your finger in her hand."

Henri put one finger in the baby's little hand. Her tiny fingers closed around it. She held on tight! Henri laughed out loud. "She likes me!" he said. He wiggled his finger a little. The baby held tighter. She made a small sound, like a happy worm squishing through the dirt.

"Can we do it again?" Henri asked. Grandma smiled. "She can follow you anywhere with that finger," she said. Henri walked his finger through the air, slow and low. The baby's eyes followed it too. At supper, Henri saved a spot on the couch for her. He held up his finger and waited, as still as a stone.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Mateo sat at the art table. He had a cracker in his hand. "Is this a square?" he asked his teacher.

"Let's find out," she said. She gave him a piece of string. Mateo laid the string along one side of the cracker. Then he laid it on the next side. It fit just the same. Side three matched too. Side four matched too. All four sides were the same. "It's a square!" said Mateo.

Next to him, a baby in a stroller watched from the doorway. The baby's big sister was painting. Mateo poured some purple paint into her cup. "Thank you," she said.

Then Mateo dipped his sponge in the purple paint. He pressed it down. It made a square print. He turned the sponge and pressed again. The square sat beside a circle and a triangle on the paper.

The baby clapped her hands. Mateo held up his purple painting. "Four sides, all the same!" he said. The baby kicked her feet and laughed.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Paisley wants to play the pretend shop at school. But Ben is already there. Ben stands behind a little box. "I am the shopkeeper," says Ben. "You can be the shopper."

Paisley wants to be the shopkeeper too. She takes the box. Ben frowns. Then she gives it back. "Okay, I shop," she says.

Ben holds up a toy banana. Paisley picks it out. She gives him a leaf for money. Ben smiles big. "Thank you, shopper!"

Paisley digs in her pocket. She finds a stinky sock. "Yuck," says Ben. "No socks in my shop." Paisley laughs and puts it away.

Then it is Paisley's turn. She stands behind the box. Ben walks down the pretend road. He shops now. "One banana, please," says Ben.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Harrison stood at the bus stop with Mama. He held her hand. The sun was warm on his toe through his sandal. "Where is the sun going?" he asked.

A big cloud moved in the sky. The cloud hid the sun. Now the sky was gray. Harrison's toe felt cool. "The sun went away," he said. "The cloud is in front of it." The wind began to blow. It blew Mama's scarf. It ruffled Harrison's hair. "Windy day," said Mama. She zipped his jacket up high.

Rain began to fall. Drop, drop, drop. Mama opened the umbrella. It went pop over their heads. "Can the sun come back?" Harrison asked. "Watch the cloud," said Mama.

They watched and waited. The bus came. The cloud moved away, slow and soft. The sun came out again. The rain stopped. Everything looked bright and shiny. Harrison smiled his sweet smile. He waved at the sun. "Hello again!" he called. The bus door opened with a hiss, and Harrison stepped up, holding Mama's hand.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Henri sat in the big waiting room. He held his doll tight. Today he would get his very first haircut. He wanted to look like Papa, but he was scared of the scissors.

"Mama, what if the hair spills everywhere?" he asked. Mama smiled. "The lady is very gentle," she said. "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut to remember it."

Henri's turn came. He sat up tall on the booster seat. The lady snipped one little curl near his ear. She held it out to Mama. Mama put the curl in a small white envelope. "Why do you keep it?" Henri asked. "So we can remember this day," Mama said.

Henri looked in the mirror. His hair was short like Papa's. He made a silly face, and the lady laughed. He waved his doll at the mirror. "We look handsome," he told the doll. On the way out, Henri held the envelope all the way home.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Leah turned three today. Her party was in the backyard. Grandma hung balloons on the fence. Friends sat near the picnic table.

Dad carried out the cake. It had three candles. Leah wanted to light them herself. She reached for the matches.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job."

Leah put her foot down with a little stomp. Then Dad lit one candle. A small flame popped up. Leah watched it flicker. Then he lit the next one, and the next. All three candles glowed.

"Now you get the big job," said Dad. "Make a wish and blow!"

Leah closed her eyes. She took a big breath. She blew out all three candles at once.

Everyone clapped. Leah hopped up and down. Mom cut the cake, and Leah got the first big piece.

"Happy birthday, Leah!" everyone said.

Leah smiled with frosting on her chin.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Beatrice went to the store with Mama and baby Sam. She had one big want. She wanted to find her small red ball. It was lost in the toy aisle.

Beatrice put toys in the basket. Sam took them out. She put them in again. Sam pulled them out again. "Silly Sam!" said Beatrice. She walked fast to the cold freezer. Sam crawled slow behind her. Mama held a hot pie near the oven area. "Careful, hot things can hurt," said Mama. Beatrice looked and did not touch.

Then Sam took a round thing out of the basket. It was red. It was her ball! "You found my answer!" said Beatrice. She laughed and clapped. "In and out are opposites," said Mama with a smile. Beatrice rolled the ball to Sam. Sam rolled it back.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Sofia wanted to make a book about her five senses. "I know eyes see," she said. "Ears hear. A nose smells. A tongue tastes." She drew them all. But one page was empty. She did not know the fifth sense yet.

Mama was in the kitchen. "Can you help me?" she asked. She put a bowl of warm oats on the table. Sofia did not touch it. "It is warm," Mama said. "Only Mama touches warm things." Sofia watched from her chair. She blew on the oats, fast fast fast, and the steam went away.

Then Mama gave her a cold spoon. Sofia held it in her fingers. The spoon felt cold. Her fingertips told her that. "We feel things by touching them with our skin," said Mama. "Like our fingertips." Sofia touched the spoon again. Cold! She touched her soft sleeve. Soft! She touched the smooth table. Smooth!

Sofia drew two hands on the empty page. "Hands feel," she said. "That is five!" She ran to the window. The moon was coming up. She touched the glass with one fingertip. It felt cool and smooth. "Good night, moon," she said. "My hands know you are there."

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Grayson ran to the window at daycare. "Look, look!" he shouted. White flakes were falling down. "It's snowy!" said his teacher, Miss Kim. "Snow pants day!" Grayson wiggled into his snow pants. He zipped up his big coat. He put on his hat. "Where are your mittens, Grayson?" Miss Kim asked. Grayson looked in his bag. No mittens! "I forgot them," he said. He felt shy about it. "You can go out anyway," said Miss Kim. "We will find a way."

Outside, the snow was deep and soft. Grayson stomped in it. Crunch, crunch! His friend Mia had red mittens. She made a snowball and threw it. "Catch, Grayson!" Grayson caught it with his bare hands. The snowball was cold. Very cold! "Brrr!" he said. His hands hurt. They turned pink. He dropped the snowball fast.

Mia looked at Grayson's cold hands. "Here," she said. She pulled off one red mitten. "Try this." Grayson put it on. Soon his hand felt warm again. "Mittens keep hands warm on a snowy day!" he said. Then Mia gave him the other mitten too. Together they made a big snowman. They glued on a paper sign that said HI. The wind blew their hats sideways. "Windy!" laughed Grayson. Inside, cocoa waited on the table. Miss Kim held the cups, one by one. Grayson wrapped both warm hands around his.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Wren sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread, but it was far away. "Dad, can you pass the bread, please?" she asked. Dad passed her the bread. "Thank you," said Wren. Dad smiled a big smile. Then he gave her some apple slices too. "Thank you," said Wren again. Dad smiled again. Wren saw that. One little word made Dad's face light up. That was fun to see.

Then Wren reached for her cup. Oops. The cup tipped over. Milk ran across the table. "Sorry, Mom," said Wren. Mom wiped the milk with a towel. "That's okay," said Mom. "Can I help?" asked Wren. "Yes, you can bring me the towel basket." Wren ran to get it. She was not lazy about it one bit. Mom wiped the table and it was dry again.

After dinner, Mom brought out a little hat. It was a tiny party hat, just for fun. Mom put it on Wren's head. "Thank you, Mom!" said Wren. Mom clapped her hands. Wren tapped the hat with one finger. The hat wiggled. Wren laughed. "Do it again," she said.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Livia looked in her toy box. "Where is Bunny?" she said. Bunny was gone. Livia wanted Bunny very much.

She looked under her bed. No Bunny. She peeked behind the curtain. No Bunny. "Bunny is not far away," said Mama. "Let's look together." They looked in the living room. They looked by the big chair.

Then Livia saw something. It was a small blue car. It was not her toy. It belonged to her brother, Sam. Sam was looking for his car. His face was sad. Livia picked up the car. She ran to Sam. "Here is your car," she said. Sam smiled big. "You gave it back!" he said. "Thank you, Livia." He gave her a hug.

Then Sam said, "Come with me." He led her to the sofa. He lifted the blanket. There sat Bunny! "I saw Bunny there," said Sam. "I wanted to give Bunny back to you."

Livia hugged Bunny tight. Bunny's soft ears were the best color in the world. "Thank you, Sam," she said. "You gave Bunny back to me." Sam held his blue car. Livia held Bunny. They sat together on the sofa. "Now we both have our toys," said Livia. Sam laughed and rolled his car along the arm of the chair.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. On Monday, Sienna and Grandma went to the market. It smelled like apples and warm bread. "Dad loved this market," said Grandma.

Sienna stopped walking. "Dad was a boy?" she asked. She could only see Dad now, tall and big. Grandma laughed. "Yes, he was little once. He was just four, like you."

They sat by the fruit stand. Grandma told about Dad's first bike. It was red, and he painted a blue star on it. He fell off far from home, and he cried. Then he got back on and rode all the way home. Sienna giggled. "Dad cried?"

"He did," said Grandma. They bought a big red apple. On Tuesday, Dad came to pick them up. "Guess what," said Sienna. "You had a bike and a star!"

Dad looked at Grandma. Grandma smiled and tapped the kitchen clock. "Time for dinner," she said. "And more stories tomorrow." Sienna took a big, crunchy bite of her apple.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Emilia sat at the big table. Mom put warm toast in front of her. Mom also put a small cup and a jug of milk. "You can do it yourself today," said Mom. Emilia wanted to do it herself. She wanted to butter her own toast and pour her own milk.

Mom gave her a knife. Mom held the knife with her, safe and slow. Emilia poked the toast with the pointy tip. The toast got a hole in it. Butter went everywhere in little bits. "That is tricky," said Emilia. "Try the flat side," said Mom. Emilia turned the knife over. She laid the flat side on the butter. She pushed it across the bread. The butter spread out. The toast looked smooth and shiny.

"Now the milk," said Mom. Emilia picked up the jug with two hands. She poured slowly. Milk went into the cup. One little drop ran down the side. She stopped and waited. Then she poured a tiny bit more. Not one drop spilled on the table.

Emilia ate her toast. An ant walked across the floor far away. "Look, Mom, I did it," said Emilia. "We can talk about it at snack time too," said Mom. Emilia took a big sip of milk.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Anthony rode the bus with Mama. He held his little red bunny. Then the bus went bump. Bunny jumped out of his hands. "Oh no," said Anthony. "Bunny is lost!"

Anthony looked under the seat. He looked in Mama's bag. Where could bunny be? A lady next to them smiled. "Look by your shoe," she said. There was bunny! The bump had made him fall. Anthony hugged him tight.

At home, Anthony found a basket. He put the basket by his bed. "This is bunny's nest," he said. Each night, bunny went in the basket. Each morning, Anthony knew just where to look. "It worked again!" he said. Was that true? He peeked in. Yes! Bunny sat there, clean and soft. "Night night, bunny," said Anthony.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Florence held Mama's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist for the very first time. "I want to be brave," said Florence. "We can go slow," said Mama.

At the dentist, a kind woman looked in Florence's mouth. "Open big," she said. Florence opened. The dentist looked and looked. Then she gave Florence a little mirror. Florence saw her own teeth. "Big smile," said the dentist. Florence smiled at herself.

On the bus home, a boy sat near Florence. He had apple slices. He bit one with his front teeth. Then he chomped it with his back teeth. The apple got small and small. "He bites first, then he chews," said Florence. Mama nodded.

At home, Florence ate fish for lunch. She bit a piece with her front teeth. Then she chewed it with her back teeth. "The fish tastes good," said Florence. She took another bite, and chewed it all up. "All done," said Mama. Florence held up her empty plate.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Leah ran to the big tree at the playground. Her friend Mia was already there.

"Let's play hide-and-seek," said Mia. "You count. We hide."

Leah put her hands over her eyes. "One, two, three, four!" She counted very fast. Then she turned around.

Mia was still standing in the open. So was their friend Sam.

"We didn't have time to hide," said Mia. "Please count slowly."

Leah hid her eyes again. "One... two... three... four... five... six... seven... eight... nine... ten." She counted slow like a snail.

Mia ran behind the slide. Sam got under the bench. Leah heard little feet on the wood chips.

She looked around. She saw Sam's shoes in a line under the bench. "Found you, Sam!"

Then she saw a happy face peeking around the slide. "Found you too, Mia!"

"Now you hide," said Mia. "I will count to ten. Slowly."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Arthur ran to Grandpa's garden. "We will plant seeds today!" said Grandpa. Arthur dug little holes in the dirt. He put tomato seeds in one row. He put carrot seeds in the middle row.

The next day, Arthur forgot his spot. "Where are my tomatoes?" he asked. Grandpa held up a stick with a tomato picture on it. He pushed it into the dirt. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," said Grandpa. Arthur clapped his hands.

Arthur made more labels with Grandpa. He drew a yellow tomato on one. He drew a long orange carrot on another. He pushed each label into the dirt, and the wind made them wiggle. Arthur watched his rows every morning. Soon tiny green leaves popped up next to every label. "Look, Grandpa! The labels found my plants!"

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay for a whole week! Juliette clapped her hands. She put on her red hat. "Let's go to the market, Grandpa!" she said. Grandpa smiled big. Off they went.

The market was loud and busy. There were apples and bread and flowers. Juliette helped pick a big green apple. "This one!" she said. Grandpa put it in the bag. They waved to the apple man. What a fun day!

At home, Grandpa took a warm bath. Juliette waited outside the door. Then Grandpa called, "Oh no! Where are the towels?" He peeked out, dripping. Juliette heard him. A problem! Grandpa was a guest. Guests don't know where things are.

Juliette ran down the hall. She opened the tall cupboard. The towels were stacked inside, soft and white. "Here, Grandpa!" she called. Grandpa took a big towel. "Thank you, my host!" he said. Juliette felt proud. She was a good host.

The next morning, Grandpa couldn't find the bathroom. Juliette showed him the door. At night, he couldn't find his slippers. Juliette pointed to the mat. "My host knows where things are," said Grandpa. Juliette grinned under her hat. Then she took his hand and said, "Come on, Grandpa. I will show you everything!"

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Owen ran to the park with Dad. He felt so excited. The swings were free at last.

Then a big dog ran up. It barked very loud. Owen felt scared. The dog looked big as a horse. Would it bite him? Owen wanted to cry.

He ran to Dad and held his hand tight. "Dad, I am scared of that dog," Owen said. "Can you help me?"

"Yes, I can help you," Dad said. "Stay right here by me."

Dad stood with Owen. The dog's owner came and called a name. "Biscuit, come here!" The dog ran to her. It wagged its tail. It did not bite anyone.

"See? Her name is Biscuit," Dad said. "She just wanted to play."

Owen watched Biscuit sniff a smelly old shoe. He laughed. That was a happy sound. Then a boy fell off the slide. He looked sad, and his sister looked angry about her dropped ice cream. So many feelings in one park, Owen thought.

Then Biscuit brought the smelly shoe back and dropped it at Owen's feet. "Thank you, Biscuit," Owen said. "But that is your shoe, not mine."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story: Penelope loved the guinea pig at school. His name was Pip. Yesterday Pip hid in his little house. Today Pip sat on the top of his hay. His food bowl was low and almost empty. "Can I feed Pip?" Penelope asked. "Soon," said Miss Amy. "First we walk to the rug for story time." Penelope sat down. She did not want to wait. She looked at the clock. The big hand moved a little bit. "Is it soon now?" she asked. "Soon means in a little while," said Miss Amy. "Not a long wait." Miss Amy read one book. Then she clapped her hands. "Story time is done. Now you may feed Pip." Penelope got the hay. She put some in the bowl. Pip ran over and began to eat. Tomorrow she would feed him again. "That was not a long wait," said Penelope. Pip made a happy squeak.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Jasmine ran to Dad with her new book. "Please read this to me!" she said. Dad sat on her bed. He opened the front of the book. He began at the first page. He read the words out loud, one by one. Jasmine looked at his finger. It moved along the little black marks. The marks told him what to say!

Jasmine turned a page. This page had no marks at all. It only showed a big rainbow in the sky. "Read this part too!" she said. Dad looked at the page. "There are no words here," he said. "There is nothing written on this page to read." So they just looked at the rainbow together.

"Can words be on the last page?" Jasmine asked. Dad turned to the back. "Yes, look," he said. There were words at the end too. Jasmine smiled. "Tomorrow can I read the words?" she asked. "You can try," said Dad. "I will help you." Jasmine hugged the book tight. "Good night, words," she said. Dad turned off the light. "Sweet dreams," he said, "my true little reader."

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Henry sat at the little red table. There was white paper in front of him. There were paint cups too.

"Today we paint pumpkins," said Miss Ana. She held up a big pumpkin. It was orange.

Henry looked in his paint cups. Red. Yellow. Blue. One, two, three. He counted them again. No orange cup. His tummy felt tight.

"I need orange," Henry said. "My pumpkin needs orange."

His friend Mia had orange paint. But Mia was using all of hers. Henry did not want to grab it. He sat and thought.

Then he looked at his brush. Red on one side. Yellow on the tip. He dipped the red brush in the yellow cup. He stirred it round and round.

The paint turned orange!

Henry stared. He touched the paint with his finger. The paint felt cool, like a tickle on his skin.

He painted a big round pumpkin. Then he painted another one. "Red and yellow made orange," he said to Mia.

"I need orange too," said Mia. Her face looked sad.

Henry pushed his orange cup across the table. "Here," he said. "You can share mine."

Mia smiled. She painted a small pumpkin next to Henry's big one. Then she put her brush down on the white paper like a pillow for it to rest.

Miss Ana came to look. "What nice orange pumpkins," she said.

Henry held up his painting. "I made orange!" he said. "Come and see!"

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Max saw the big red truck at school. He wanted it right now.

Tom had the truck first. Max grabbed for it. The truck fell on the pillow corner and one wheel went click. Tom held the truck to his chest.

Max sat on a small pillow. His sweater felt itchy. He put his hands in his lap. He waited. He counted one, two, three.

Tom drove the truck to the rug. "You can have a turn now," said Tom. Max held out his hands. Tom put the truck in them.

"Thank you, Tom," said Max. Tom smiled a big smile. Then Tom gave Max a surprise. A little blue car from his own pocket.

"My turn now," said Max. He put the truck down next to the blue car. "You can have them both."

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Riley sat on the blue rug at school. Miss Kim held up a big card. It had a big A on it. "A says ah," said Miss Kim. "Ah, ah, apple," said Riley.

Then Miss Kim opened a book. Riley pointed at a small word. "That little one is not A," said Riley. "A is big. That one is small." Miss Kim smiled. She put the card next to the book. The small a sat under the big A. Riley looked and looked. She waited. Then she put her finger on both letters. "Same letter," said Riley. "Big A. Small a. Both say ah."

Riley went to the wall. The wall had big letters all across it. She found the small a in her book again. She held the book up high. The small a sat under the big A on the wall. "Ah," said Riley. "Ah, ah, apple."

At dinner that night, Riley saw a box on the table. "That is a big A," she said. "And that is a small a. Same letter." She tapped the box two times. "Ah, ah," she said, and took a big bite of her apple.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
David waited by the gate at school pickup. He wore his green hat. His tummy made a little growl. "Lunch soon," said Mama. "First we go home."

At home, David ate his sandwich. Then he played in the sand. His socks got sandy. His pants got muddy too. Mama said, "Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket so they can be washed." David looked at the big basket.

David made a game. He held his sandy sock. He tossed it. It went in the basket. "Goal!" said David. He tossed the other sock. It went in too. Then his muddy pants went in. Mama smiled. She took the basket to the washing machine. Soon the clothes would be clean. David got dressed in soft blue pajamas. "Bath first," said Mama, and she turned on the warm water.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Sadie sat at the dinner table. She wanted to go to Mia's house. "Can we go now?" she asked. "Now it is dinner time," said Mom. "You slept last night. That was yesterday." Sadie looked at her plate. Yesterday she had peas. Today she had carrots. The carrots were orange. What a nice color!

"But I want to go today," said Sadie. "Today is now," said Dad. "Tomorrow comes after today. Tomorrow is the day after today." Sadie counted on her fingers. Yesterday, today, tomorrow. Three days! "What comes after tomorrow?" she asked. "Another tomorrow," said Dad with a smile. Sadie laughed.

"After I sleep, it will be tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Then you wake up. Then we go to Mia's house." Sadie ate her carrots. One, two, three carrots. She would sleep, and then it would be tomorrow. She felt happy. "Tonight I will sleep fast," said Sadie. Dad gave her a big hug. "Sleep first," he said. "Mia tomorrow."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Charlie was so excited. Today he would write his name! He grabbed a pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard on the paper. The letters came out big and wiggly. "Yucky," said Charlie. "That is not my name."

Miss Amy sat down next to him. "Watch me," she said. She pinched the pencil between her thumb and her first finger. Then she let it rest on her middle finger. She wrote Charlie's name, C-H-A-R-L-I-E, one letter at a time.

Charlie tried it. Thumb, first finger, middle finger. Pinch and rest. He lifted the pencil and made a C. Then an H. Then A, R, L, I, E. Seven letters!

"Look, Miss Amy!" said Charlie. "That says Charlie!"

He held up his paper like a flag on a road. "Can I do it again?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Jayden sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. The paper pumpkin had no color yet. Grandma gave him a plate with paint on it. "Look," she said. "Red, blue, yellow, green."

Jayden looked and looked. He wanted orange for his pumpkin. He saw no orange paint. He said, "I need orange. One, two, three, four paints. No orange anywhere."

"Try two paints together," said Grandma.

Jayden put his brush in the red. He put his brush in the yellow. He stirred them on the plate. Red and yellow made orange! "Orange!" said Jayden. "Red and yellow made orange!"

He painted his pumpkin all orange. The stem he painted green. Then he used blue for the sky behind it. "My pumpkin looks so good," said Jayden. "Not bad at all!"

Grandma smiled and clapped. Jayden held up his wet painting. "Red and yellow," he said. "One more time, tomorrow!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Amira wanted to find the kittens. Mama said they were in Room Five. But the doors all had marks, not words.

Amira looked at a door. It had a 5 on it. She held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. The 5 and her five fingers matched! She knocked on the door.

Papa opened it. "Amira, you found the kittens," he said. "How did you know?" Amira showed her hand. "This door has a five," she said. Papa smiled. "That is the same five."

Inside, the kittens sat in a box. Their little paws went scratch, scratch on the cardboard. Amira counted them. "One, two, three." Then she counted their ears. "One, two, three, four, five, six."

Mama came in with warm milk. She set it down far from Amira. "Let it cool," she said. The kittens drank and drank. Amira counted their tails, one, two, three. Then she counted to ten on her fingers, just for fun.

The smallest kitten looked up at her with big new eyes. It wobbled to the edge of the box. "Hello, little one," Amira said. She counted its whiskers, one by one.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Aurora sat at the dinner table. Something smelled good. Her nose knew it first. "What is that smell?" she asked. "Soup," said Mom. Aurora heard it bubble. Her ears heard the pot pop and puff.

Dad put three things by her plate. "Close your eyes and guess," he said. "Use your fingers." Aurora shut her eyes tight. Her fingertips touched something bumpy. "A pinecone!" Next her fingertips felt something soft. "A feather!" Last came something smooth and cool. "A rock!" Dad said, "Yes! Your fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy."

"How do they know?" asked Aurora. She touched the pinecone again. The bumpy bumps tickled her fingers. "They just know," she said.

Mom set the soup in the middle of the table. Aurora dipped her spoon. Her tongue tasted carrots. She painted a carrot mark on her bread with the tip of the spoon. "My mouth knows carrots," she said, and she touched the pinecone one more time, just to feel the bumps again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Camille put on her warm coat. She was going to the hockey rink with Dad. There was a game on the ice, but today the rink had a fun corner for little kids. A red hoop lay on the floor. A big soft ball sat in a basket. Camille wanted to win a sticker.

First she tried the beanbag. She threw it from far away. It missed the hoop. It landed on the cold floor. She ran and got it. She threw it again. It missed again.

"Can I try from here?" Camille asked.
"Sure," said Dad. "Try it!"

Camille took three little steps. Now she stood close to the hoop. She tossed the beanbag. It went in! The beanbag sank right into the middle of the red hoop.

"It went in!" she shouted. She jumped up and down.

Then Dad rolled her the big ball. She held out both hands. The ball was soft and pretty and blue. She squeezed it to her chest like a blanket. "I caught it!" she said.

Dad clapped his hands. "You did it, Camille!"

A helper gave Camille a shiny star sticker. Camille stuck it on her coat. She ran back to the hoop with the beanbag. "Watch me!" she said. She stood close and tossed. In it went again!

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Jasmine wanted tea for her bear. She found two cups on the playroom shelf. One cup was big. One cup was small. The small cup had nothing in it. The big cup had nothing in it too.

Daddy brought a pot of warm water. It was not hot like tea for grown-ups. It was just warm, like a bath. Daddy poured slow, slow, slow. The small cup filled up. Jasmine held her bear's cup. It was empty, so empty. She poured too fast. Water ran over the top. "Oh no," said Jasmine. Daddy gave her a towel. She wiped the little puddle.

Jasmine tried again. This time she poured slow. She watched the water climb. She stopped before the top. Now the cup was full. "Look, Bear," she said. "Your cup is full now." She took a tiny pretend sip. "Yummy," she said. "Just a little sour, like lemon tea." Then she tickled Bear with a string from her pocket, fast, fast, fast, and Bear got a big hug, slow and cozy.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Quinn went to the pet store with Dad. She saw fish, birds, and one small kitten. The kitten was gray with white paws. It looked at Quinn. "Can we take it home?" Quinn asked. "Yes," said Dad. "It will be your first pet."

Dad got a box with holes for the kitten to ride in. He got food in a little bag. He got two small bowls too. "One for food," said Dad. "One for water." At home, Dad put the bowls on the floor. The kitten drank some water. Then it went to sleep.

The next morning, Quinn ran to see the kitten. The kitten was at its water bowl. The bowl was empty. The kitten looked up at Quinn. It looked sad. "Dad!" Quinn called. "The water is all gone!"

Dad came with Quinn to the sink. He held the bowl under the tap. Fresh, clean water filled it up. Quinn helped Dad carry it back. She could not reach the floor from up high, so Dad set it down. The kitten drank and drank. Then it rubbed on Quinn's leg and purred. "Fresh water every day," said Dad. "That is your job, Quinn." Quinn smiled and petted the kitten's soft head.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Felix sat in his car seat. The road was bumpy. Bump, bump, bump went the wheels. "Look," said Mama. "One cow. Two horses. Three ducks." Felix saw them all in the green field. "Ducks say quack," said Felix. Then his tummy made a little rumble. Mama gave him a banana from the food bag. It was yellow and soft.

Soon the car stopped. They were at the library. "I want a book about animals," said Felix. "Like the ducks and the cow." A kind librarian heard him. "Come with me," she said. She walked to a shelf. "Here are all the animal books, in a group." Felix touched the spines. One, two, three, four books. He picked a big one with a cow on the front.

Mama found toy books on another shelf. "Toys are in a group too," she said. Felix hugged his cow book. On the bumpy ride home, he turned the pages. The last page showed a duck. Under the duck was a tiny frog. "A surprise!" said Felix. He laughed all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Alice pushed her baby doll in one little swing. She wanted her friend Max to push the other swing. But Max was on the steps. He was counting them so he could jump down. "One, two, four," said Max. Alice stopped pushing. "You went one, two, four," she said. "Is that right?" she asked herself. She sang her counting song in her head. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." "Three," said Alice. "Three comes before four."

Max tried again. He stepped on each step and said each word. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." He had counted all ten steps. He jumped down with a soft bump onto the wood chips. Alice clapped. Max ran to the swing. Alice pushed one swing and Max sat in the other. "Dream swings," said Alice. "Side by side." Max touched the wet slide. "It feels slimy," he said, and wiped his hand on his shirt. They swung high together, counting one, two, three.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Hayden went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about a cat. He looked at shelf one. He looked at shelf two. No cat book. He looked at shelf three. Still no cat book.

The librarian came over. "Can I help you?" she asked. "Yes, please," said Hayden. "I want a cat book." The librarian found one with a cloudy blue cover. "Would you like a sticker, too?" she asked. "No, thank you," said Hayden. The librarian smiled a big smile.

Then Hayden saw his friend Mia. Mia offered him a cracker. Hayden did not like crackers. "Yuck!" he shouted. Mia's face looked sad. Hayden tried again. "No, thank you," he said softly. Mia smiled and ate the cracker herself. Hayden held his cat book tight. "Thank you," he told the librarian. She waved as he walked out the door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Brooks had a cough. Mom said, "Let's get your medicine." They went to the pharmacy down the street.

The pharmacy had bright lights. There were bandages and soap and little bottles on shelves. Brooks saw a big bottle of cough medicine on the counter. He reached up his hands.

The pharmacist shook her head gently. "Only a grown-up gives a child medicine," she said. Brooks put his hands down. He waited by Mom's coat.

Mom picked up the bottle. She read the label slowly. Then she filled the small cup. She poured it carefully. The medicine was purple. Brooks looked at it.

"Show me how you drink it," Mom said. Brooks took the little cup from her hand. He sipped the purple medicine. It tasted like grapes.

They walked home in the soft light of night. Mom said, "That was your last spoonful." Brooks yawned. At home, his cough was quieter. His teddy sat by his bed. Mom tucked the blanket up to his chin.

"Night night, bear," Brooks whispered. He closed his eyes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Louis stood at the little table. The toast sat on his plate. He held the butter knife. The teacher had given him soft butter. Louis spread it slow. He pushed the knife across the bread. The butter made the toast shiny. "Look at me," said Louis.

Next came the milk. The carton was big for his hands. He tipped it over his cup. Milk came out fast. A drop ran down his hand. Louis took a breath and tipped it slower. The milk went in, not one drop on the table. His friend Mia clapped. "Good pouring," she said.

Louis set the milk on the table. He started to run off to play. Then he stopped. He looked at the milk. "The milk goes back in the fridge," said Mia, "to keep it cold." Louis picked up the carton. He carried it to the fridge, one careful step at a time. He put it on the shelf and shut the door. "Far from warm, nice and cold," he said. Then he ran back to chase Mia around the table, laughing, his toast waiting on his plate.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Connor wanted to build a big tower in the playroom. He pulled a heavy box of blocks. He pulled and pulled. The box would not move. "Why won't you go?" he asked. The box was heavy.

Then he saw a feather pillow on the chair. He picked it up. Up it came, so easy! "Heavy and light are opposites," said his sister, popping her head in the door.

Connor wondered about the blocks. Maybe he could take some out. He used a small tool, a toy shovel, to scoop blocks out. The box got lighter. Now he could pull it! He stacked the blocks fast. The tower grew tall. Then it fell down slow, block by block. "Again!" said Connor. He put the pillow on top, so soft and light, and started once more.
